cards.front: Why does the ozone layer in the stratosphere matter to people and other living things on the ground?
cards.back: **Ozone** absorbs all of the most energetic UV-C and most UV-B from the Sun, so less harmful radiation reaches the surface and damages the DNA of living cells.
cards.hint: Think about what sunscreen does for your skin.

cards.front: Which human-made chemicals cause stratospheric ozone loss, and which element do they release?
cards.back: **Ozone-depleting substances**, such as CFCs, release chlorine (or bromine) in the stratosphere and break ozone down faster than natural processes can replace it.
cards.hint: Name both the chemical and the element.

cards.front: Why can a single chlorine atom destroy so many ozone molecules?
cards.back: Chlorine is a **catalyst**: it takes part in the reactions but is regenerated unchanged, so one atom can repeat the cycle and destroy a very large number of ozone molecules.
cards.hint: Think about whether chlorine is used up.

cards.front: What are the four steps of the chlorine cycle that destroys ozone?
cards.back: 1) A chlorine atom takes an oxygen atom from an ozone molecule. 2) This forms **chlorine monoxide** and an ordinary oxygen molecule, $\mathrm{O_2}$. 3) Chlorine monoxide reacts with a free oxygen atom. 4) The chlorine atom is released and attacks another ozone molecule.
cards.hint: Four steps, starting with a chlorine atom.

cards.front: What are chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), and where were they once used?
cards.back: **CFCs** are human-made compounds of carbon, chlorine and fluorine, once common in refrigerators, aerosol sprays and foam plastics.
cards.hint: Think of a fridge and a spray can.

cards.front: Why do CFCs reach the stratosphere even though they are released near the ground?
cards.back: CFCs are very **unreactive** in the lower atmosphere, so they do not break down or wash out. Winds slowly carry them up into the stratosphere, a journey that can take years.
cards.hint: Consider what stops them being removed lower down.

cards.back: A large area of **severely thinned** stratospheric ozone over Antarctica that appears each spring.
cards.hint: Think about where and when it is seen.

cards.front: What harmful effects follow from ozone depletion for humans, plants and marine life?
cards.back: More UV-B reaches the surface, raising the risk of skin cancer and cataracts in humans. Plant growth and crop yields can fall, and **phytoplankton**, which support ocean food chains, can be harmed.

cards.front: A student says ozone depletion is the same thing as global warming. What is wrong with this?
cards.back: Depletion mainly **raises UV-B** at the surface, while warming is mainly caused by greenhouse gases that trap heat. They are separate problems with different causes.
cards.hint: Ask what each process mainly changes.

cards.front: A student says ozone is always beneficial. What is the error?
cards.back: Ozone in the **stratosphere** protects life, but ozone near the ground is a harmful pollutant. The same gas has different effects depending on where it is.
The **1987** international agreement that commits countries to phase out the production and use of ozone-depleting substances, using binding targets with timetables.
cards.hint: Consider the year it was agreed.

cards.front: What special support did developing countries receive under the Montreal Protocol?
cards.back: They received **longer deadlines** for phasing out ozone-depleting substances, along with financial help.
cards.hint: There were two kinds of support.

cards.front: Why have replacement chemicals for CFCs brought new problems?
cards.back: Some contain no chlorine, so they spare ozone, but many are strong **greenhouse gases** that trap heat. CFCs also last for decades, so ozone recovers only slowly.
